<proposed_plan>
# Finish encrypted-backup PR #12895

## Current findings

[PR #12895](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12895) has six distinct issues across seven unresolved review threads. Greptile failed; Bugbot finished with findings; CodeRabbit remains pending. The green `complete` job is a preflight placeholder—build/tests did not run for this stacked base.

No edits or pushes have been made in this Plan-mode session.

## Fixes

- **Restore only the selected checkpoint.** Resolve the machine and checkpoint selector from metadata before decrypting. Preserve existing numbering and selector behavior; corrupt or unreadable sibling checkpoints must not block restoration.
- **Replace backups atomically.** Prepare every replacement locally, then submit replacements and stale-ref deletions in one atomic push. As selected, unsupported servers fail clearly without changing existing refs. Record the new scheme and uploaded set only after success; retries after interrupted status persistence must remain safe.
- **Preserve previously uploaded history.** Retain the existing cutoff when reconfiguring the same origin. Migration must include previously uploaded, locally retained, still-eligible checkpoints even when they precede the cutoff. Preserve normal privacy and retention exclusions.
- **Validate backup identity.** Check the header against the ref’s machine ID and UUID, then compare decrypted checkpoint identity and timestamp with the header before creating or reusing a plaintext wrapper. Reject mismatches. This provides consistency checking, not sender authentication.
- **Verify restorability accurately.** Share one age/SSH restorability helper between doctor and connection disclosure. Use a small in-memory encryption/decryption probe with loaded identities so unrelated, locked, or mismatched SSH keys cannot produce a success claim.
- **Bound payload processing.** Enforce limits before allocation and Git writes: 256 MiB encrypted/compressed input, 1 GiB decoded payload, and 100,000 files. Bound MessagePack collection decoding and reject unsafe paths, duplicates, and unsupported modes. Apply matching upload limits so mise cannot create backups it refuses to restore.

## Wording and interfaces

- Remove the unsolicited “Not an experimental feature” statement and equivalent promotional wording from the authored PR description. Keep tests proving operation with experimental settings disabled and preserve the existing env-directive gate.
- Correct blog PR #99: explicit `--recipient` values select the recipient set rather than automatically adding to defaults.
- Document atomic migration requirements and payload limits. Keep existing CLI flags and backup format; add only internal selection, validation, and atomic-push interfaces.
- Continue on the existing PR branch, preserving its `bootstrap/10-auto-sync` base and ready-for-review status.

## Validation and completion

- Add regression coverage for corrupt siblings; metadata/ref mismatches; unrelated and locked SSH identities; oversized payloads; failed atomic pushes; unsupported atomic servers; retry after interruption; and migration preserving older uploaded checkpoints.
- Run the encrypted-backup and neighboring sync, onboarding, rollback, and age e2e tests through mise tasks.
- Complete the unfinished no-default-features check with `RUSTFLAGS=-D unused`, settings/doctor unit tests, formatting, scoped lint fixes, and Clippy without exclusions.
- Push verified fixes with conventional commits and update the PR description with actual results.
- Explicitly dispatch the test workflow on the PR branch because automatic PR tests target `main`.
- Monitor checks and paginated review threads for the updated head until they settle. Address valid new findings, inspect detailed logs for failures, and report any external blocker accurately. Do not merge.
</proposed_plan>

<proposed_plan>
# Finish #12895 with hardware-backed age encryption

## Summary

Extend this PR with user-installed age plugins for [macOS Secure Enclave](https://github.com/remko/age-plugin-se) and [Linux TPM](https://github.com/Foxboron/age-plugin-tpm), alongside the existing backup correctness fixes.

Hardware-only recipients are allowed with a device-loss warning. Restored files and local checkpoint caches remain plaintext, as selected.

## Hardware support

- Enable the Rust age library’s plugin support. Accept plugin recipients through existing `--recipient` arguments and plugin identities through existing age identity-file settings. Use age’s plugin protocol rather than implementing platform cryptography.
- Require users to install plugins and generate hardware identities themselves. Document Secure Enclave and TPM setup, public-recipient export, and configuring multiple recipients.
- Keep explicit recipients authoritative. Do not silently add a software key or fall back to plaintext when a plugin is unavailable.
- Execute plugins only from locally configured recipients or identities; remote backup metadata must not select executables.
- Allow interactive restoration to request Touch ID or PIN through plugin callbacks. Cancellation and unavailable hardware produce actionable errors without modifying restored files.
- Keep status, doctor, and watcher diagnostics noninteractive. Report hardware identities as configured but unverified; do not decrypt a test payload during routine diagnostics. Background encryption must reject interaction requests instead of waiting for input.
- Warn when configuring hardware-only backups that device loss can prevent recovery. Recommend an independently stored recovery recipient without generating or requiring one.
- Preserve plaintext local restoration caches. Explain that hardware authorization protects initial decryption, not subsequent access to restored data.

## Backup correctness and wording

- Select the requested checkpoint before decrypting, so unreadable siblings cannot block restoration.
- Build replacements before one atomic push containing updates and stale-ref deletions. Unsupported servers leave existing backups intact. Persist migration success only after the push succeeds.
- Preserve previously uploaded, retained, eligible history during scheme changes; do not advance the cutoff when reconnecting the same origin.
- Validate machine ID, checkpoint UUID, and timestamp across ref, header, and payload before materialization or cached reuse.
- Correct age/SSH restorability checks; distinguish verified software identities from unverified hardware identities.
- Bound encrypted/compressed input to 256 MiB, decoded payload to 1 GiB, and file count to 100,000. Enforce matching upload limits and validate paths, modes, and duplicates before writing Git objects.
- Remove unnecessary “not experimental” wording while retaining experimental-disabled tests and the env-directive gate.
- Correct blog #99’s recipient wording and document hardware setup, recovery recipients, atomic migration, and plaintext local caches.

## Validation and completion

- Add plugin-protocol fixtures covering mixed recipients, missing plugins, cancellation, malformed responses, noninteractive failures, and recovery with the software recipient when hardware is unavailable.
- Add regressions for sibling corruption, identity mismatches, SSH restorability, payload limits, failed atomic migration, retry after interruption, and preservation of older backups.
- Verify real Secure Enclave and TPM round trips where hardware is available; explicitly report any hardware coverage unavailable locally.
- Run focused unit/e2e tests, the unfinished no-default-features and settings/doctor checks, formatting, scoped lint fixes, and Clippy without exclusions.
- Continue on the existing PR branch and stacked base. Push verified changes and explicitly dispatch build/test CI, since automatic PR tests target `main`.
- Once GitHub’s API rate limit clears, refresh feedback and monitor the final pushed head until checks and reviews settle. Address valid findings and report external blockers; do not merge.
</proposed_plan>
how does hardware encryption work with syncing? is it just that it doesn't? or could we have multiple consumers with different hardware keys?

Yes—**multiple machines can each use their own hardware key to decrypt the same backup.**

Age encrypts each checkpoint with a random symmetric key, then wraps that key separately for every recipient. For example, one backup can include:

- Your Mac’s Secure Enclave public key.
- Your Linux machine’s TPM public key.
- An offline software recovery key.

Any one matching private key can unlock the backup. Private hardware keys stay on their respective devices; you only share public recipients.

Automatic backup uploads use those public keys, so they don’t require unlocking the receiving hardware. Restoration uses the recipient machine’s hardware and may request Touch ID or a PIN. Secure Enclave recipients support encryption from other machines, including Linux. [Plugin documentation](https://github.com/remko/age-plugin-se)

The distinction is that **this PR encrypts recovery backups**. The shared configuration branch still syncs in plaintext. Multiple recipients let multiple machines restore encrypted backups; they don’t make the shared configuration sync encrypted.

Adding a new machine’s recipient requires re-encrypting existing backups if it should read them. Removing a recipient protects rewritten and future backups, but cannot revoke access to old copies that recipient already has.
does this pr include the ability to encrypt files instead of just backups?

No. This PR encrypts **remote recovery backups only**. The shared configuration branch, local history, and restored files remain plaintext.

Mise already has experimental age-encrypted `[env]` values, but that’s separate from encrypting whole dotfiles.

Encrypting selected files during normal sync—with decryption when applying them—would be an additional feature. The multiple-recipient hardware-key approach could support it.

<proposed_plan>
# Finish #12895: encrypted sync files and hardware-backed backups

## Configuration and behavior

- Add `encrypt = true` to dotfile policies, defaulting to false. It protects tracked file contents and source files used by copy, symlink, and template entries during publication.
- Use **one shared public-recipient list**, `[history.encryption].recipients`, for all encrypted synced files. No per-file overrides.
- Keep backup recipients in machine-local `[history.origin]` configuration. Existing `origin set --recipient` continues to configure backups.
- Files, rendered outputs, and local recovery history remain plaintext locally.
- Missing keys or failed decryption pause applying and publishing for the whole setup. Fetching and local history continue. Report which files require unlocking without exposing their contents.

Example:

```toml
[history.encryption]
recipients = ["<mac-public-recipient>", "<linux-public-recipient>"]

[dotfiles]
"~/.config/app/credentials" = { mode = "track", encrypt = true }
```

## Encrypted file synchronization

- Encrypt selected file contents before building a publication commit. Preserve logical filenames; document that paths, configuration, and recipient public keys remain visible.
- Store versioned encrypted envelopes at their existing branch paths. Bind each envelope to its logical path and original file mode.
- Upgrade the setup repository marker when encrypted files are first published. Read existing format-1 repositories; older clients must reject the new format rather than apply ciphertext as files.
- Decrypt upstream files before the existing reconciliation and conflict logic. Keep plaintext comparison state local and ciphertext publication state separate. Reuse ciphertext when content, mode, and recipients are unchanged so repeated syncs produce no churn.
- Preserve existing conflict decisions and configuration validation. Never apply ciphertext to a destination or merge ciphertext as text.
- Encrypt template sources before publication and decrypt before rendering. Reject `encrypt = true` for inline `content`/`block` declarations, whose secrets would otherwise remain in shared configuration; direct users to external sources.
- Preserve privacy exclusions: encryption does not implicitly enable sharing of private files. Reject overlapping declarations that would publish the same source both encrypted and plaintext.
- Prevent backup bypasses: files marked encrypted must be excluded from plaintext remote backups, including when rebuilding older checkpoints. They may enter encrypted backups under that machine’s backup recipients.
- Recipient changes re-encrypt all current encrypted files in one leased branch update. Missing decryption access blocks the change. Explain that changing encryption cannot erase plaintext or revoked recipients’ access from earlier Git history and clones.

## Hardware-backed identities

- Support user-installed age plugins for Secure Enclave and Linux TPM through the existing recipient and identity configuration.
- Users install plugins and generate hardware identities themselves. Accept software and hardware recipients together; hardware-only lists are allowed with a device-loss warning.

## Encrypted shared files

Set `encrypt = true` on a dotfile declaration to encrypt its contents on the
setup branch. All encrypted files use one shared public-recipient list:

```toml
[history.encryption]
recipients = ["<age-or-plugin-public-recipient>", "<recovery-public-recipient>"]

[dotfiles]
"~/.config/app/credentials" = { mode = "track", encrypt = true }
"~/.config/app/config" = { source = "templates/app.tera", mode = "template", encrypt = true }
```

Tracked files and external sources are encrypted before publication and decrypted
before application or template rendering. Filenames, public recipients, and mise
configuration remain visible. Inline `content` and managed blocks cannot use this
option: move sensitive contents into an external source. Encryption does not
change `share = false` or privacy exclusions.

Live files, template outputs, local history, and decrypted recovery caches remain
plaintext. Encrypted files are excluded from plaintext remote recovery backups;
encrypted recovery backups use the machine-local recipients configured through
`origin set --encrypt-backups --recipient …`, independently of shared-file readers.

If an incoming file cannot be decrypted, publication and application pause for the
whole setup. Local history and fetching continue. Run `mise bootstrap dotfiles
pull` with a matching identity to unlock incoming content. Unchanged encrypted
content does not create a fresh commit on every sync.

Changing the shared recipient list re-encrypts current encrypted files in one
branch update. Existing Git history and clones are not rewritten: enabling
encryption cannot erase earlier plaintext, and removing a recipient cannot revoke
access to copies already encrypted for it. Repositories using encrypted shared
files use setup format 2; older mise clients stop with an upgrade message.

### Hardware identities

Install an age plugin yourself and generate its identity using the plugin's
instructions: [Secure Enclave on macOS](https://github.com/remko/age-plugin-se) or
[TPM on Linux](https://github.com/Foxboron/age-plugin-tpm). Use the exported **public
recipient** in the shared list or backup `--recipient` options, and configure the
local identity file with `settings.age.identity_files`. Plugin binaries must be
available on PATH. Mise does not provision hardware keys or install plugins.

Multiple recipients can decrypt independently: for example, a Mac's Secure
Enclave, a Linux TPM, and an offline software recovery identity. Keep an independent
recovery recipient: losing hardware can make hardware-only data unrecoverable.
Explicit `--recipient` arguments replace backup defaults rather than adding to them.

Interactive restoration may request Touch ID or a PIN. Background work never
starts hardware identity plugins; status and doctor report them as configured but
unverified. Once decrypted, the local cache may be reused without hardware access.

### Encryption limits and backup replacement

Encrypted payloads are limited to 256 MiB of ciphertext/compressed data and 1 GiB
of decoded data; a backup contains at most 100,000 files. Creation and restoration
both enforce these limits.

Changing backup encryption prepares replacement commits locally and then replaces
recovery refs using an atomic Git push. The server must support atomic pushes;
otherwise the operation fails while retaining existing refs. Previously uploaded,
locally retained eligible checkpoints remain included when reconfiguring the same
origin, even without `--include-existing`.
